title: Jet Lag and Alcohol: Does Drinking on a Flight Make It Worse?
excerpt: Does alcohol make jet lag worse? How drinking on a long flight affects your sleep, hydration, and body clock, whether alcohol hits harder at altitude, and how to recover faster.
metaDescription: Does alcohol make jet lag worse? How drinking on a plane affects sleep, hydration, and your body clock, plus how to drink smarter when you travel.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol makes jet lag worse, not better. A drink or two on a long flight feels like it should help you sleep, and it often does knock you out for a while. But alcohol breaks up the second half of your sleep, dries you out in an already very dry cabin, and adds a hangover on top of a body clock that's already confused. The result is that the first day or two at your destination usually feels rougher, not smoother. You don't have to fly dry to travel well, but timing and amount matter a lot more in the air than they do at home.

**The quick rules:** Keep it to one or two drinks on a long flight, and have them early in the flight rather than right before you try to sleep. Match every drink with a full glass of water. Don't mix alcohol with sleeping pills or strong antihistamines on a plane. When you land, use daylight, meals, and bedtime at local time to reset your clock, and save the celebratory drinks for your second or third night, once your sleep has started to settle.

> **When to see a doctor.** Jet lag itself is temporary and harmless, but some symptoms after a long flight are not. **Get medical care right away if** you notice swelling, pain, warmth, or redness in one calf or thigh (a possible blood clot), sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, coughing up blood, fainting, or confusion that doesn't clear. See a doctor before your next long trip if you have heart or lung disease, sleep apnea, a history of blood clots, or take medicines that interact with alcohol. If you're drinking heavily every day while traveling and notice shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you go without, say so plainly to a doctor. Those are signs your body has become used to alcohol, and stopping suddenly can be risky. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.

## What Jet Lag Actually Is

Jet lag is a mismatch between your internal body clock and the clock on the wall where you've landed. Your body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle called a circadian rhythm. A small group of cells in the brain acts as a master clock, and it uses light, especially morning daylight, as its main signal for what time it is. That master clock then sets the timing for sleepiness, alertness, body temperature, hunger, digestion, and the release of hormones like melatonin (which tells your body it's night) and cortisol (which helps you wake up).

When you cross several time zones quickly, the outside world jumps ahead or behind, but your internal clock doesn't. It shifts gradually. A common rule of thumb is that the body adjusts by about one time zone per day, though this varies a lot between people and depends on direction. Until it catches up, you're trying to sleep when your body thinks it's mid-afternoon and stay awake when it thinks it's 3 a.m.

Common jet lag symptoms include:

- Trouble falling asleep at night, or waking up very early and not getting back to sleep
- Heavy daytime sleepiness, especially in the afternoon
- Poor concentration and slower thinking
- Irritability and low mood
- Stomach problems, such as constipation, loose stools, or no appetite at odd times
- A general feeling of being unwell or "off"

### Why flying east is usually harder

Most people find flying east (for example, from the US to Europe) harder than flying west. Flying east means you need to go to bed earlier than your body wants to, and most people's internal clock naturally runs a little longer than 24 hours, so it's easier to stretch the day than to shorten it. Flying west means staying up later, which most people find easier. This matters for drinking, because an eastbound red-eye is exactly the flight where people order a drink to try to force sleep.

### Jet lag versus travel fatigue

Not all post-flight misery is jet lag. Travel fatigue is the tiredness, headache, and stiffness from the trip itself: early alarms, airport stress, cramped seats, dry air, and poor sleep in an upright position. You can get travel fatigue on a long north-south flight with no time change at all. It usually clears after one good night's sleep. Jet lag lasts longer because it's a timing problem, not just a tiredness problem. Alcohol makes both worse.

## Does Alcohol Make Jet Lag Worse?

Yes, in several ways that stack on top of each other.

### 1. It wrecks the quality of the sleep you do get

Alcohol is a sedative, so it can help you fall asleep faster. That's why a drink on a plane feels like it's working. The problem comes later. As your body breaks the alcohol down over the next few hours, it has a rebound effect: sleep gets lighter and more broken, you wake up more often, and you get less REM sleep (the dreaming stage that matters for memory and mood). Research on alcohol and sleep has found this pattern consistently, with sleep being heavier in the first half of the night and more disrupted in the second half.

On a flight, you're already sleeping badly because of noise, light, and an upright seat. Alcohol takes that poor sleep and makes it worse. You arrive having technically slept, but feeling as if you didn't. For more on why this happens, see our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### 2. It may interfere with your body clock's own signals

Your body clock relies on melatonin rising in the evening and falling in the morning. Some research suggests that alcohol can lower or shift melatonin release, and animal studies suggest alcohol can affect the clock genes that keep the circadian rhythm running. The human evidence here is less settled than the evidence on sleep quality, so it's fair to say alcohol probably doesn't help your clock adjust and may slow it down. What's clear is that it adds another confusing signal to a system that's already trying to recalibrate.

### 3. It dehydrates you in the driest place you'll ever sit

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it, you urinate more than you drink. On the ground, that's mild. In an airplane cabin, the air is very dry because outside air at cruising altitude holds almost no moisture, and cabin humidity on long flights is commonly well below what you'd find in a typical home. You're already losing water through your breath and skin. Adding alcohol makes dehydration more likely, and dehydration brings headaches, fatigue, and dizziness that blur straight into jet lag symptoms. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains the mechanism in more detail.

### 4. You land with a hangover on top of jet lag

Even a moderate amount of alcohol can leave you with mild hangover symptoms: headache, nausea, low energy, and poor focus. Jet lag causes almost the same list. When the two combine, you feel worse than either would make you feel alone, and you're less likely to do the things that actually fix jet lag, like getting outside in morning daylight and staying awake until local bedtime.

## Does Alcohol Hit Harder on a Plane?

This is one of the most common questions about drinking while flying, and the answer has two parts.

**Your blood alcohol level is not dramatically higher at altitude.** Studies going back decades have generally found that the same amount of alcohol produces a similar blood alcohol level in the air and on the ground. The idea that one drink on a plane equals two or three on land is a myth.

**But you may feel the effects more.** Commercial cabins are pressurized, but not to sea level. They're usually kept at the equivalent of about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, which is roughly like being in a mountain town. At that pressure, the oxygen level in your blood drops a little. Most healthy people don't notice. Add alcohol, and the combination can leave you more lightheaded, foggy, and tired than the same drinks would on the ground. Dehydration, an empty stomach, and being short on sleep all add to that.

There's also some newer research that's worth knowing about. A 2024 study published in the journal *Thorax*, by researchers at the German Aerospace Center, had healthy young adults sleep in a chamber set to typical cabin pressure after drinking alcohol. Compared with sleeping sober at normal pressure, the combination lowered their blood oxygen levels during sleep and raised their heart rate. It was a small lab study, not a real flight, but the authors suggested limiting alcohol on long flights, especially for people with heart or lung conditions. Our guide on [drinking at high altitude](/never-hungover/altitude-alcohol-high-elevation-drinking-safety-2025) covers the effects of lower oxygen in more detail.

## Is It Okay to Drink on a Long Flight?

For most healthy adults, one or two drinks on a long-haul flight is not dangerous. It's just not helpful for jet lag. If a glass of wine with your meal is part of what makes a flight bearable, here's how to keep the damage small.

- **Drink early, not late.** Have your drink with the first meal service, not right before you try to sleep. That gives your body time to clear some of it before the sleep you care about.
- **Keep it to one or two.** The effects on sleep and hydration grow with the amount.
- **Match each drink with water.** A full glass of water for each drink, plus water regularly throughout the flight, is a simple habit that helps.
- **Eat something with it.** Food slows the absorption of alcohol and makes you less likely to feel the altitude effect.
- **Skip it on an overnight eastbound flight if sleep is the goal.** This is the flight where your sleep quality matters most, and where alcohol does the most harm to it.
- **Move around.** Get up and walk the aisle every hour or two when it's safe, and flex your calves while seated. Long periods of sitting still are a known risk factor for blood clots in the legs. Alcohol can make you sleep more deeply in one position and get up less.

### Don't mix alcohol with sleep aids on a plane

This is the one firm "don't." Many travelers take something to help them sleep on a flight: a prescription sleeping pill, an anti-anxiety medicine, or an over-the-counter sleep aid containing a sedating antihistamine like diphenhydramine or doxylamine. All of these add to alcohol's sedating effect. Together, they can make you far more drowsy and confused than you expect, slow your breathing, and make you unsteady on your feet in a moving aircraft. They can also make it harder to wake up and respond in an emergency. If you plan to use a sleep aid on a flight, skip the alcohol entirely. See our guide to [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) for a fuller breakdown.

> **Talk to your doctor** before combining alcohol with any medicine on a flight, including sleep aids, anxiety medicines, motion-sickness tablets, or pain relievers, and before a long trip if you have heart disease, lung disease, sleep apnea, or a history of blood clots.

## Melatonin, Alcohol, and Jet Lag

Melatonin is the supplement most often recommended for jet lag, and there's reasonable evidence behind it. A Cochrane review (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002) looked at controlled trials and concluded that melatonin taken close to the target bedtime at the destination was effective at reducing jet lag, especially for people crossing five or more time zones and flying east. Low doses seemed to work about as well as higher ones for shifting the clock, while higher doses were slightly more sedating.

The catch is that melatonin and alcohol don't pair well. Alcohol may blunt your body's own melatonin, which works against the whole point of taking it. Both also cause drowsiness, so combining them can leave you groggier than either alone. If you're using melatonin to adjust to a new time zone, the sensible approach is to take it on nights when you haven't been drinking, or at least to keep drinks light and early in the evening. Our guide on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) covers timing and safety in more depth.

As with any supplement, check with a doctor or pharmacist before using melatonin if you take blood thinners, blood pressure medicines, diabetes medicines, or seizure medicines, or if you're pregnant.

## What About Coffee?

Caffeine can be a real help with jet lag when it's well timed. A coffee in the morning at your destination can help you stay alert and push through to local bedtime. But caffeine has a long tail. It can stay in your system for many hours, so an afternoon coffee to fight jet-lag sleepiness can make it harder to sleep at the new local bedtime. Using alcohol at night to come down from caffeine during the day sets up a cycle where neither your sleep nor your clock settles. Our guide on [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) explains why that pairing backfires.

A good rule for the first few days: coffee before lunchtime, local time, and none after.

## How to Beat Jet Lag Without Relying on Alcohol

The most effective jet lag tools are simple and free. They work by giving your body clock strong, consistent signals about the new local time.

### Before you fly

- **Shift your schedule a little in advance.** For eastbound trips, go to bed and wake up an hour earlier each day for a few days beforehand. For westbound trips, go later. Even a partial shift helps.
- **Arrive rested.** Starting a trip short on sleep makes jet lag worse. Late packing nights and early airport runs are a common cause of a bad first day.
- **Go easy the night before.** A big send-off night before an early flight means boarding dehydrated and underslept, which is the worst starting point for jet lag.

### On the plane

- **Set your watch to destination time** as soon as you board, and start thinking in that time zone.
- **Sleep or stay awake based on destination time.** If it's night where you're going, try to sleep. If it's daytime there, try to stay awake.
- **Use an eye mask and earplugs** to make cabin sleep possible.
- **Drink water steadily.** Bring an empty bottle through security and refill it.
- **Keep alcohol and caffeine small, and well away from the time you want to sleep.**

### When you land

- **Get outside in daylight.** Light is the strongest signal your body clock has. After flying east, morning light at your destination helps pull your clock earlier. After flying west, afternoon and early evening light helps push it later.
- **Eat meals at local times.** Meal timing is another signal your body uses to set its clocks, especially for digestion.
- **Stay awake until a reasonable local bedtime.** If you have to nap, keep it short, ideally under about 30 minutes and before mid-afternoon.
- **Be active.** A walk outside combines light and movement, two of the best tools you have.
- **Keep the first night light on alcohol.** This is when your sleep is most fragile. One drink with dinner is a very different night from a late round of welcome drinks.

### For short trips

If you're only away for a day or two, it may make sense not to adjust at all. Keeping your home schedule as much as possible, and scheduling important meetings during your home-time daytime hours, can be easier than shifting your clock and then shifting it back. In that case, alcohol at what is "night" locally but "afternoon" for your body is especially likely to backfire. For more on staying sharp on work trips, see our [business travel survival kit](/never-hungover/business-travel-dhm-survival-kit-2025).

## Drinking After You Land: Vacation, Weddings, and Work Trips

Many long trips are built around drinking: a wine-country holiday, a destination wedding, a conference with an open bar. You don't have to sit those out. A few adjustments make a big difference.

- **Give yourself a lighter first night.** Your first night's sleep at the new time zone is the one that sets up the rest of the trip. Keep drinks lighter that night, and plan the big night for later.
- **Watch your tolerance.** Being short on sleep and dehydrated can make the same number of drinks feel stronger than at home.
- **Count drinks, not hours.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. Pour sizes abroad are often different from what you're used to, so a glass of wine or a cocktail may hold more alcohol than you expect.
- **Eat and hydrate.** A real meal before drinking and water between drinks help both the hangover and the jet lag.
- **Protect the morning.** Getting into daylight the morning after is one of the best things you can do for jet lag. A heavy hangover makes it much more likely you'll sleep through it.

If you regularly need a drink to fall asleep on trips, it's worth noticing. Alcohol tends to work less well as a sleep aid the more often you use it, and the sleep it gives you is lower quality. That's a good conversation to have with a doctor, who can suggest better options for travel sleep.

## Who Should Be Most Careful About Drinking on Flights

Some people should be more cautious about alcohol on a plane, or skip it:

- **People with heart or lung disease,** because of the extra dip in blood oxygen at cabin pressure.
- **People with sleep apnea,** because alcohol relaxes the airway muscles and can make breathing pauses worse, and sleeping upright in a seat may already be harder.
- **People with a history of blood clots, recent surgery, pregnancy, or on hormone therapy,** because of the higher clot risk on long flights. These travelers should talk to their doctor about prevention before flying.
- **Anyone taking medicines that interact with alcohol,** including sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, some antidepressants, and some antibiotics.
- **Anyone who will be driving after landing.** Jet lag and alcohol both slow your reactions. Combined, they make driving from the airport a real safety risk.

## Does DHM Help With Jet Lag?

There's no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) helps with jet lag itself. Jet lag is a body clock problem, and no supplement for alcohol fixes that. Light, meal timing, sleep timing, and possibly melatonin are the tools with evidence behind them.

Where DHM may fit is the alcohol side of the trip. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. Some travelers take it on trips where they expect to drink, such as a wedding or a holiday dinner, hoping to feel a bit better the next morning. It does not undo the effects of alcohol on your sleep or hydration, and it isn't a reason to drink more on a flight.

If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence. If you take medication, check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol makes jet lag worse. It breaks up your sleep, dehydrates you in a dry cabin, may interfere with your body clock's signals, and adds a hangover to jet lag symptoms.
- Your blood alcohol isn't much higher at altitude, but lower cabin oxygen can make you feel the effects more.
- One or two drinks early in a long flight, with water and food, is reasonable for most healthy adults. Skip alcohol on an overnight flight where sleep matters, and never combine it with sleep aids.
- The real jet lag fixes are daylight, meals and sleep on local time, short naps, and possibly melatonin on alcohol-free nights.
- Keep your first night at the destination light on drinks, and save the big nights for later in the trip.
- Get medical help right away for calf swelling or pain, chest pain, or sudden shortness of breath after a flight.

For the science on how alcohol disrupts sleep stages, which is part of why it makes jet lag worse, see our deep dive on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol make jet lag worse?**

Yes. Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it makes sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night and reduces REM sleep. It also adds to dehydration in a dry airplane cabin and can leave you with a mild hangover. Together, these make the first day or two after a long flight feel worse, and they make it harder to do the things that fix jet lag, like getting into morning daylight.

**Does alcohol affect you more on a plane?**

Your blood alcohol level after a given amount is generally about the same in the air as on the ground, so one drink doesn't equal two. But cabins are pressurized to the equivalent of about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, which slightly lowers the oxygen in your blood. Combined with alcohol, dehydration, and poor sleep, that can make you feel more lightheaded and tired than the same drinks would at home.

**Is it okay to drink alcohol on a long flight?**

For most healthy adults, one or two drinks on a long flight is not dangerous, but it doesn't help jet lag. Drink early in the flight rather than right before sleeping, have a glass of water with each drink, eat something, and get up and walk around regularly. Skip alcohol if you're taking a sleep aid, and talk to your doctor before flying if you have heart or lung disease, sleep apnea, or a history of blood clots.

**Will a drink help me sleep on an overnight flight?**

It may help you fall asleep, but the sleep you get will usually be worse. As your body processes the alcohol, sleep becomes lighter and more broken. On an overnight flight, especially one heading east, that sleep is important for adjusting to the new time zone. An eye mask, earplugs, and setting your schedule to destination time usually work better than a drink.

**Can I take melatonin and drink alcohol for jet lag?**

It's better not to combine them. Alcohol may reduce your body's own melatonin, which works against the supplement, and both cause drowsiness. If you're using melatonin to adjust to a new time zone, take it on nights when you haven't been drinking, or keep drinks light and early. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take other medicines.

**How long does jet lag last?**

It depends on how many time zones you crossed, which direction you flew, and the person. A common rule of thumb is about one day of adjustment per time zone crossed, with eastbound trips usually taking longer. Getting daylight, eating, and sleeping on local time speeds things up. Heavy drinking in the first few days tends to slow it down.

**What's the best way to drink on vacation without making jet lag worse?**

Keep your first night light, because that sleep sets up the rest of your trip. Eat before drinking, drink water between drinks, watch for larger pour sizes abroad, and get outside in morning daylight the next day. Save the big nights for once your sleep has started to settle, usually after the first two or three days.

**Does DHM help with jet lag?**

There's no good evidence that DHM helps with jet lag, which is a body clock problem. DHM has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. Some travelers use it on trips where they expect to drink, but it doesn't undo alcohol's effects on sleep or hydration.
